title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
data_curation: Training uses REDSearcher_RL_1k, 1,000 challenging deep-search tasks with ground-truth answers; no new data is constructed. The agent has two tools, search (Serper) and visit (Jina Reader). Reward is a binary outcome from an LLM judge (deepseek-v4-flash, temperature 0.0, max 10 output tokens, thinking disabled) that accepts equivalent wording, aliases and abbreviations against the ground truth. The same ground-truth answer is also used to build the dense session-level signal: the teacher-forced average log-likelihood of the answer tokens under the pre-update actor, appended after a fixed 'Now there's enough information to answer.' continuation.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. Training is a single RL stage from Qwen3.5-4B for one epoch (63 rollout iterations) with rollout batch 16 prompts x 8 samples (global batch 128), run in a colocated setup that alternates rollout and training phases to isolate the optimization signal from asynchrony. Settings: Adam at constant LR 1e-6, betas (0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.01, clip 0.2/0.28, KL coefficient 0.001 (low-variance estimator), no entropy bonus, on 8 GPUs with TP=2 and CP=4.
method: Defines Multi-Session Agentic RL, where a trajectory is a set of sessions (normal, compaction, subagent), each trained as a separate segment, and replaces the common broadcasting baseline (copying the trajectory advantage to every session) with critic-free hierarchical credit. (1) Session-aware trajectory advantage: within success and failure subgroups, session count N_i is mapped to a centered rank u_i in [-1,1], and A_sat = (1 - rho*u_i)*A_traj with rho=0.2, so successful trajectories with fewer sessions and failed trajectories with more sessions get higher advantage without flipping sign. Homogeneous groups use fallbacks -beta1*u_i (all-success, beta1=0.2) and beta0*min(u_i,0) (all-failure, beta0=0.1). (2) Session-level shaping: each non-terminal session's reward is the stop-gradient change in answer-likelihood potential between its output and input states, normalized within the prompt group separately by session type, and added as A_traj + lambda_r*r_hat (lambda_r=0.1), with an all-failure gate and a direction-preserving gate. Compaction allows up to 10 summaries per rollout; forking allows 1-3 non-nested subagents per call and up to 10 calls, with 128K tokens per session.
eval_metrics: Accuracy and average sessions per trajectory on BrowseComp (1,266 questions) under single-session, multi-session/compact and multi-session/subagent inference, against base Qwen3.5-4B, single-session GRPO, IGPO (turn-level information gain) and multi-session Broadcasting. Base: 23.22 / 24.80 / 21.64; GRPO: 31.99 / 34.68 / 31.91; Broadcasting: 35.31 (3.17 sessions) compact, 31.44 (4.43) subagent; Mosaic: 38.86 (2.35) compact, 32.46 (3.77) subagent. Session-utility metrics are Positive-IG rate (compact 59.92% vs 47.74% for Broadcasting) and IG per session (0.89 vs 0.86). Ablations show both components help, with a larger combined gain for linear compaction than for DAG-like subagent trajectories.
key_results: On BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B, Mosaic reaches 38.86% accuracy under context compaction versus 35.31% for broadcasting (a 10.1% relative gain) while cutting average sessions from 3.17 to 2.35, and 32.46% versus 31.44% under subagent forking with 3.77 versus 4.43 sessions. It also beats IGPO (31.36 / 24.64) with much lower information-gain computation time.
evolution_note: Mosaic extends GRPO-based agentic RL (Search-R1-style search agents) to trajectories broken by context compaction and subagent forking, which modern harnesses produce but single-session RL assumes away. It reacts to broadcasting used in harness-agnostic trainers such as Dressage and Polar, and moves IGPO's turn-level information-gain reward to the session level with type-conditioned normalization. The paper frames session utility and allocation, cross-session state transfer, and asynchronous or black-box-harness multi-session RL as open directions.
